verses.translation_literal: Of David. Judge me, YHWH, for I, in my integrity I have walked, and in YHWH I have trusted; I will not slip.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of David. Judge me, LORD. I ask it with open hands. I have walked the whole road in wholeness, and every step of it I leaned on you. I trust you, and so I will not slip.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a courtroom opening, but the defendant is asking for the verdict, not fleeing it. 'Judge me' (shafteni) is a request for a ruling in the speaker's favor, the way a wronged party in the ancient Near East appealed to a king or a god as the final judge. Play it as confidence, not bravado: the next verses show he expects the examination to hold up. The word 'integrity' (tom) is wholeness, a life with no seam between inside and out, not sinlessness. The Hebrew has an emphatic 'for I, in my integrity' with the pronoun placed before the phrase, which sets him against the crowd of verses 4–5. The KJV 'therefore I shall not slide' invents a result: the Hebrew simply has two clauses side by side, 'I have trusted in YHWH; I will not slip'. The verb ma'ad is to give way underfoot, the loose stone on a mountain path, and it sets up the image of the level ground in verse 12. KJV also renders the verbs 'I have walked / I have trusted' as simple pasts, which fits, but it adds 'also', which is not in the Hebrew. Rashi, followed by Radak, notices the tension with Psalm 143:2, 'do not enter into judgment with your servant', and resolves it by saying David asks to be judged beside the wicked, not beside the righteous.

philological_notes.note: Judge, rule on my case. In a dispute the shofet does not only punish but also puts the wronged party right, so the sense runs from 'give me a hearing' to 'vindicate me'. Ibn Ezra reports two readings: 'take my case against my enemies', or 'take the judgment away from me if my heart has turned from you'.
Integrity, wholeness; the noun tom comes from the root 'complete'. Ibn Ezra links it with 'be whole' (tamim) in Deut 18:13, 'You shall be whole with the LORD your God'.
To slip, to have one's footing give way; Metzudat Zion glosses it as sliding and being dislodged from a place. The motion is physical, which the 'level ground' of verse 12 answers.

verses.translation_literal: Test me, YHWH, and try me; refine my kidneys and my heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: Test me, LORD. Try me. Put me in the fire and look at what is left. Refine my kidneys and my heart.
verses.directors_commentary: Three verbs of assay in a row, each from the workshop or the market: bachan (test, as a metal or a coin is assayed), nasah (put to the proof), and tzaraf (smelt, refine in the crucible). The speaker is not asking for comfort; he is offering himself to the furnace, and the actor must not flinch on 'refine'. 'Kidneys' is the word the KJV turns into 'reins', an archaic English that a modern audience no longer hears as a body part. In the Hebrew thought-world the kidneys are the hidden seat of conscience and emotion, the place where a person is driven from within, and 'kidneys and heart' together mean the whole inner man, as in Jeremiah 11:20. The ASV and BBE cover the body word with 'mind' and 'thoughts' and lose the bodily bluntness. The Qere (the reading tradition) has the imperative 'refine', a plea; the written text, as Radak notes, has an extra waw that would make it 'refined', a claim. YLT follows the claim. Either way the picture is metal in fire: the dross burns off and only the true silver remains.

philological_notes.note: Kidneys, the deep inner organs and the seat of hidden motive and conscience; the standard pair is 'kidneys and heart'. Radak, citing the Talmud (Berakhot 61a), says the kidneys give counsel and the heart understands.

Smelt, refine: the goldsmith's word, used of purifying silver in a crucible. The Qere is an imperative; the Ketiv (as Radak reads it) has an added ו that reads as 'refined', so the verse changes from request to claim.

token_glosses.gloss: and put me to the proof

verses.translation_literal: For your steadfast love is before my eyes, and I have walked about in your truth.
verses.translation_dramatic: For your steadfast love stands before my eyes, and in your truth I have walked, to and fro, all my days.
verses.directors_commentary: This verse says why he can stand the test: not because he is strong, but because he keeps looking at something outside himself. 'Before my eyes' (leneged einai) means in plain view, the thing he steers by. Chesed is the covenant loyalty that YHWH keeps; the KJV 'lovingkindness' is a Coverdale coinage that sounds sweeter than the Hebrew, which is about faithfulness to a binding promise. Emet, the second word, is 'truth' but also reliability, what holds up under weight: the same root as 'amen'. The verb 'I have walked' here is in a form (hitpael) that means a habitual, back-and-forth walking, not a single march, which is why YLT has 'walked habitually'; the KJV flattens it to a plain past. It is the verb used of Enoch and Noah, who 'walked with God' (Gen 5:22, 6:9), and Radak points to Noah. The audience would hear a person whose daily route is set by YHWH's character.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, steadfast love: kindness that rests on a standing bond. Meiri reads it here as the favors YHWH has done for him, kept constantly in mind so that he does not give up serving.
Hitpael of 'walk': to walk about, to go to and fro, a habitual way of life. Ibn Ezra glosses it as making a custom of a way, citing 'and Enoch walked' (Gen 5:22); Radak cites Noah (Gen 6:9).

verses.translation_literal: I have not sat with men of falsehood, and with those who hide themselves I do not go in.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have never taken a seat among the men of emptiness. I do not slip through the door to join those who hide their faces.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm turns from the speaker's inner life to the company he refuses. Two verbs of social belonging: 'sit' (yashav), to take a place in a gathering, and 'go in' (bo), to enter the room. The verse is built as a chiasm in Hebrew: 'not I sat with men of falsehood / and with the hidden ones not I enter', so the two negatives frame the two groups. 'Men of falsehood' (metei shav) is a phrase the KJV softens to 'vain persons'. Shav is emptiness, the lie, the worthless thing, and it is the word in the commandment about taking YHWH's name 'in vain'; 'vain' in modern English means conceited and misses the point. Metei is an old plural of 'men' (as in 'few men', Gen 34:30, which Metzudat Zion cites). The second group, 'those who conceal themselves', does their business out of sight. The KJV 'dissemblers' is accurate and Rashi explains who they are: those who go in secret to do their deeds in the dark, citing Isaiah 29:15. Radak adds a motive: he refuses lest he learn their ways.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'men of emptiness/falsehood'. Metei is the construct plural of the noun mat, 'man', as in 'men of number' (Gen 34:30), per Metzudat Zion. Shav' is vanity and falsehood, the word of the third commandment.
Those who hide, who keep themselves concealed; Rashi and Radak read them as people who do wrong in secret, and Meiri as pious frauds.

verses.translation_literal: I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and with the wicked I will not sit.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have hated the gathering of those who do harm, and I will not sit down with the wicked.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb is plain and hard: 'I have hated' (sane'ti). Modern readers wince, and translators often cushion it; the BBE has 'I have been a hater of the band of wrongdoers'. Do not cushion it in performance, but give it its object: he hates not people in general, but the 'assembly' (qahal) of evildoers, a rival congregation set against the assemblies (makhelim) of verse 12, from the same root, where he will bless YHWH. 'Assembly' is the word for Israel gathered before God, and he refuses a gang that mimics it. The two halves are a pair: 'evildoers' (mere'im) names those who do harm, 'the wicked' (resha'im) those who are guilty in a legal sense. Ibn Ezra gives a neat ladder across verses 3–5: walked, sat, entered, and now sat again; he reads 'men of falsehood' as wicked in speech and 'the wicked' as wicked in deed. The KJV 'congregation' is exact, but the Hebrew sounds like a political or military muster as well as a religious one.

philological_notes.note: The assembly of those who do evil. Qahal is the word for the covenant community gathered, so this names a counter-congregation. Mere'im is a Hiphil participle: those who make or do evil.
The wicked, the guilty. Ibn Ezra distinguishes them from the men of falsehood: those are wicked in speech, these in deed.

verses.translation_literal: I will wash my palms in innocence, and I will go around your altar, YHWH,
verses.translation_dramatic: I will wash my hands clean, in innocence, and then I will walk the circle of your altar, LORD,
verses.directors_commentary: Now the scene moves from the street to the sanctuary, and the speaker acts out a rite. Washing the hands before approaching the altar is the priests' practice (Exodus 30:19–21), and here the washing is done 'in innocence': no water is mentioned, and the washing is the clean life itself. Malbim says as much: he does not wash with water from the basin but with being free of sin. The KJV 'I will wash mine hands in innocency' is faithful, but it adds 'so' before 'will I compass', which makes the second act a consequence; the Hebrew has a plain 'and', and the sense is order (first clean, then approach), which Metzudat David puts as 'without cleanness the offering is not accepted'. 'Compass' (asovevah) means to circle, to go around: it is a procession around the altar, not the 'compassing' of modern speech; the ritual is not fully described in the Torah, so the actor should not invent a choreography beyond a slow walk around the altar's four sides. The kaf is the palm, the cupped part of the hand that holds the gift. Rashi's aside is practical: the commandments must be kept without theft, as a stolen lulav is invalid (Sukkah 3a), so cleanness is tied to honest hands.

philological_notes.note: Innocence of my palms; the noun means being free of guilt. Malbim reads the washing as the cleansing of the soul, not of the hands with water. Rashi: no theft in the commandments I perform.
To go around, to circle. The cohortative ending marks resolve: 'let me go around'. Radak links it with bringing burnt offerings.

verses.translation_literal: to make heard with a voice of thanksgiving, and to recount all your wonders.
verses.translation_dramatic: so that I may send a voice of thanks out across the court, and tell, one by one, all your wonders.
verses.directors_commentary: The sentence has no subject or main verb of its own: it hangs from the walk around the altar, and says what the walk is for. Two infinitives, 'to make heard' and 'to recount', and both are public acts. He is not praying silently; he wants the sound of thanks to carry. The preposition matters: he makes heard 'with a voice of thanksgiving', the voice is the instrument. Todah is the thank-offering, and the word for the song that goes with it, so 'voice of thanksgiving' means the sound of that rite. The KJV 'publish with the voice of thanksgiving' is accurate in its old sense of 'make public'; modern ears hear a book, so the dramatic layer says 'send out'. The first verb is oddly spelled, without the usual ה of the Hiphil, and Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all read it as 'to cause to be heard', Radak citing Isaiah 23:11, 'to destroy', spelled the same way. 'Wonders' (nifla'ot) are the things that go beyond ordinary experience, the rescues the speaker has lived. Radak says he will tell them before the congregation, aloud, about the kindnesses that saved him.

philological_notes.note: Short form of le-hashmia', 'to cause to be heard'; the heh of the Hiphil is dropped. Parallel: Isa 23:11 'to destroy'.
Your wonders: acts too great for ordinary explanation. Rashi hears in 'all' a hymn that reaches back to the past and forward to the days of the Messiah; I give it only as his reading.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, I have loved the dwelling of your house, and the place of the tabernacle of your glory.
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD, I have loved the home that is your house, the place where your glory pitches its tent.
verses.directors_commentary: After the hate of verse 5 comes the love, and the pairing is deliberate: Ibn Ezra says it answers 'I have not sat with men of falsehood'. The speaker names two things he loves, both by their word for 'dwelling'. Ma'on is a home, a lair, a settled habitation, and mishkan, from the root 'to dwell', is the word for the tent-shrine; together they describe the sanctuary as the place where YHWH lives, and the verse says kavod, 'glory', not the 'honour' of the KJV. Kavod is weight, the heavy visible presence that filled the tabernacle (Exod 40:34), and 'honour' reduces it to reputation. The Hebrew 'the place of the tabernacle of your glory' is a stack of three nouns in construct, an almost architectural phrase, and the actor should let each noun land. Radak identifies the house as the place where the ark stood and the Levites and prophets served; Malbim says he comes out of love, not habit. For a modern audience the claim is that this is where the speaker feels most at home.

philological_notes.note: Dwelling, residence; Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as a residence. Often used of God's heavenly or earthly home.
The tabernacle of your glory. Radak says the glory dwelt where the ark was, upon the prophets and men of the holy spirit.

verses.translation_literal: Do not gather my soul with sinners, nor my life with men of blood,
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not sweep my soul away with sinners, nor my life with the men of blood.
verses.directors_commentary: The prayer turns to the future and to the end. 'Gather' (asaf) is the verb for harvest and for being gathered to one's people at death, so the plea has a double edge: do not let me share their company, and do not let me share their end. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as death, and Metzudat David as a death like the sinners', and the dramatic layer lets that sense show. The pairing is the Hebrew's own: 'soul' (nefesh) and 'life' (chayyim), two words for the same person, set against 'sinners' and 'men of blood'. The KJV 'bloody men' is close, but 'bloody' in English is now a mild curse; the Hebrew says anshe damim, men of bloodshed, those who spill blood. The second clause borrows its verb from the first, a gapped construction: 'Do not gather ... nor my life with men of blood'. Meiri points out that the 'not' reaches across. Nefesh is often the living self, the whole person who breathes and wants. Radak and Meiri hear more in this verse: Radak reads it as the fate of the soul after death, 'my soul will be gathered to your glory when I die', and Meiri as the prayer that the soul not perish with the flesh as the sinners' does. The KJV 'soul' can carry either reading; an actor should choose one and let the other echo.

philological_notes.note: Gather, collect (a harvest, a camp); of a person, to be gathered to one's kin in death. Metzudat Zion glosses it as death.
Men of bloods: the plural damim is bloodshed, the blood of violence. Stronger than KJV 'bloody men'.

verses.translation_literal: in whose hands is a scheme, and their right hand is full of a bribe.
verses.translation_dramatic: men with a scheme in their hands, and a bribe filling their right hand to the brim.
verses.directors_commentary: A short, bitter portrait of the men he does not want to join. The picture is of hands, and the actor can use them: a plan in the hands, money filling the right. Zimmah is the key word, and the KJV 'mischief' is vague. Rashi says every zimmah in Scripture means 'plan', for good or evil, while Radak and the common sense of the word in Leviticus and Hosea make it an abomination, a shameful deed; this verse can bear both, a scheme carried out by the hand. 'In their hands' can also mean 'in their power': Radak cites 'in his hand' as 'in his possession' (Gen 24:10), so the hands hold wealth they have taken. Shochad, the bribe, is the crime the Torah names as blinding the wise (Exod 23:8, Deut 16:19): it buys the judge, which is why it sits here after the prayer 'judge me' in verse 1. The right hand is the hand of power and of the oath; 'full' (mal'ah) is a feminine verb with 'right hand', agreeing with a feminine noun. The speaker asks to be judged by a God who cannot be bought.

philological_notes.note: A plan, plot, or shameful act. Rashi: in the Bible it always means a thought, for good or evil. Radak: an abomination or evil deed, as in Hos 6:9; here he reads it as the killing and striking that the hands do.
A bribe, a gift that perverts judgment. Its place in the verse makes a link with the plea 'judge me': the speaker wants a judge who takes no bribes.

verses.translation_literal: But I, in my integrity I will walk; redeem me and be gracious to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I will go on in my integrity. Redeem me, LORD, and be gracious to me.
verses.directors_commentary: The 'But I' (va-ani) answers the men of the last verse, hands against hands: theirs full of a bribe, his walking in wholeness. It repeats the opening of the psalm, 'in my integrity', and closes the circle with a switch of tense: in verse 1 he has walked, here he will walk. The verse shifts from claim to petition without a pause, with two short commands. The first, 'redeem me' (pedeni), is the language of ransom: to pay the price that frees a captive or a firstborn. The KJV's 'be merciful unto me' for the second is fair, but chanan is grace given freely to someone who has no claim on it, which sits oddly after eleven verses of claiming integrity. Play that: a man who insists on his clean hands finishes by asking for a gift. Radak reads 'redeem me' as from troubles, and Metzudat David as from the death of the sinners. Meiri sees the logic: because he plots no counter-schemes, he needs God's help.

philological_notes.note: Redeem, ransom: free by paying a price. Radak: from troubles; Metzudat David: from the death of the sinners.
Be gracious to me, show me favor that is not owed. Radak ties it to God's goodness, shown when he sees the integrity of the heart.

verses.translation_literal: My foot has stood on level ground; in assemblies I will bless YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: My foot stands on level ground. And in the great gatherings I will bless the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends on its opening image, now at rest. Verse 1 said 'I will not slip' (ma'ad); verse 12 gives the ground that answers it: mishor, level, even, open country, a road with no stones to turn the ankle. The Hebrew verb is a perfect, 'has stood': the foot has already taken its stand, as if the prayer of the last verses were answered in the speaking. Rashi reads it as 'on a straight path'. The KJV 'standeth' flattens the perfect into the present, and 'an even place' is good, though the Hebrew word also carries the sense of uprightness, which YLT brings out with 'uprightness'. The last line moves from the private foot to the public voice: 'in assemblies' (makhelim), a rare plural that means the gatherings of the people, and it reverses the evil assembly (qahal) of verse 5. The Targum adds 'of the righteous', but the Hebrew has no qualifier. Place the actor's feet flat: the blessing is spoken from firm ground, to a crowd.

philological_notes.note: On level ground, on a smooth road; also uprightness and justice. Rashi: on a straight way. The word resolves the image of slipping in verse 1.
In assemblies, in the gatherings of the congregation: a plural form of the 'assembly' (qahal) word. Meiri reads it as 'in public, with a great noise'.
